title.en: The Drunken Sculptor and the Sand-Spreading Hen
title.zh: 醉酒的塑者與撒沙的母雞

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (the spot where the hen spread the sand, the hole of Osha)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（母雞撒沙之地、奧沙聖泉之穴）

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XIII

summary.en: At first there was no earth: only Okun (Olokun), the ocean, a water stretched over all things, with Olorun above it, coeval and all-containing. Olorun summoned his elder son Orishalla, gave him some earth and a hen with five fingers, and bade him go down and make the earth upon Okun. On the way Orishalla found palm-wine, drank, slumbered; and Olorun called the younger son Odudua, who descended, laid the sand on the sea, and set the five-fingered hen on it — she scratched and spread the sand, forcing the water aside. Ilife was the spot where this took place, round which at first the sea still flowed; Odudua ruled the land as its first king, and the sea ran away through a small hole — the Osha, whence to this day one fetches holy water, much water and it never fails. Then Orishalla, wrathful at losing the creation, made war on Odudua; they contended long, made peace, and went underground together, never to be seen again.
summary.zh: 太初無陸地，唯有奧貢（奧洛貢）——漫蓋萬物的汪洋，其上為奧洛倫，二者同生並包羅萬有。奧洛倫召長子奧里夏拉，授以泥土與一隻五趾母雞，命他下去在奧貢之上造陸。途中奧里夏拉拾得棕櫚酒，飲醉酣眠。奧洛倫改召次子奧杜杜瓦；他下凡將沙鋪於海面，放上五趾母雞——母雞抓散沙土，逼水退讓。伊費正是此事發生之地，四圍海水環流；奧杜杜瓦為此地首王，海水則從一處小孔退去——即「奧沙」，至今取之不竭的聖水之穴。奧里夏拉憤而與奧杜杜瓦開戰，久戰言和，二人一同入地，從此不見蹤影。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the first of Frobenius's three Ife creation versions (1910-12) — the Ife-Benin city version, distinct from the coastal (Ellis) Yemaja-cycle. Oduduwa is here a male God, as Frobenius notes for the interior. Cross-refs: yoruba-ife-creation, obatala-creation.

passages.text: At first there was no earth. There was only Okun (or Olokun), the ocean, a water stretched over all things. Above it was Olorun. Olorun, the Orisha of the sky, and Olokun, the Orisha of the sea, were coeval. They contained (or possessed) all that there was. Olorun had two sons. The first one's name was Orishalla (the same as Otaballa, who here is also simply called Orisha); the younger's, Odudua. Olorun summoned Orisha. He gave him some earth. He gave him a hen with five fingers. He said to him, "Climb down and make the earth upon Okun." Orisha went. On the way he found some palm-wine. He began to drink and got drunken. Then he slumbered.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIII (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Olorun saw this. Then Olorun summoned Odudua and said to him: "Thy (elder) brother has got drunken on his way down below. Go thou, take the sand and the hen with five fingers and make the earth upon Okun." Odudua went. He took the sand. He went down and laid it on the sea. He put the hen with five fingers on it. The hen began to scratch and spread the sand about and forced the water aside. Ilife was the spot where this took place, round which, at first, the sea still flowed. Odudua ruled the land of Ilife as its first king. The sea of Olokun grew less and less and ran away through a small hole from there, a hole from which to this day one can fetch the holy water — much water and it never fails. It is called Osha. Now, Orisha was very wrath that he had not created the earth; he began to wage war against Odudua. They contended for a long time, but then made peace. They both went underground and were never seen again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIII (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Mirror of Awo-Aje, and the Stone Brothers of Ife
title.zh: 埃沃-阿傑之鏡與伊費石像兄弟

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (the stones worshipped where the two workers finished their labours)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（二神完工化石受祭之地）

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XIII

summary.en: In the second version, Olorun sent down Oshalla with a ball of sand: "Spread this out upon the face of the waters." Oshalla picked up a flask of palm-wine on the road and drank whenever he was athirst, until he grew weary, went to sleep and forgot his errand. Then the other Orishas took a mirror (Awo-aje), looked into it, and saw him drinking down below, asleep; whereupon Olorun sent Odudua, a strong man, who made the earth and pushed the water aside, and to him Olorun gave the five-fingered hen that pushed the water back so that it became the sea. When the two had finished their work they went into the earth at Ife where they had begun their labours, and were turned to stone; since then men have worshipped those stones — and Odudua is so greatly feared that before anyone in Ife may speak his name, a sheep must be slain and its blood drunk.
summary.zh: 第二版本中，奧洛倫遣奧夏拉攜一團沙下凡：「把沙鋪在水面上。」他在路上拾得一瓶棕櫚酒，渴即痛飲，倦極入睡，竟忘了神命。諸神取出「埃沃-阿傑」之鏡照看，見他在下界飲酒酣眠、有負所託。奧洛倫於是改派壯士奧杜杜瓦——他造陸退水，又獲五趾母雞把水推回成海。功成之後，二人走進伊費他們始工之地，化作石頭；世人自此拜石為神。奧杜杜瓦威嚴可畏——伊費人欲提其名，必先宰羊飲血。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; second Ife creation version (Frobenius 1910-12). The name-taboo (sheep sacrifice before speaking Odudua's name) is an etiological custom detail. Cross-ref: yoruba-oduduwa-sand-hen.

passages.text: In the beginning the earth was not. There was only water. Olorun sent down Oshalla. He gave him a ball of sand on his way. He said: "Spread this out upon the face of the waters." Oshalla went. On the road Oshalla picked up a flask of palm-wine. He tasted it and said: "This is good." He drank while going. Whenever he was a-thirst he drank a mouthful. Then he grew weary, went to sleep and forgot what Olorun had bidden him. Then the other Orishas took a mirror (Awo-aje), looked into it and saw that Oshalla had been drinking down below, gone to sleep and forgotten Olorun's behest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIII (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Thereupon Olorun sent Odudua, saying: "Do thou what I told Oshalla to do." Odudua was a strong man. He took a ball of earth with him. He descended. He made the earth and pushed the water aside. Olorun then gave Odudua a hen, called Adje-alesse-mahun; it was a hen with five fingers; it pushed the water back so that it became the sea. When Odudua and Oshalla had finished their work, they went into the earth at Ilife where they had begun their labours, and were turned to stone. Since then men worshipped these stones. Odudua is greatly feared. So powerful is this Godhead that before the people in Ife can speak the name of Odudua, they must slay a sheep and drink its blood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIII (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Island in the Waters: Olorun Founds Ife and Seats the Sixteen
title.zh: 水中之洲——奧洛倫奠伊費、安十六神

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (the hill of the three palms, navel of the Yoruba universe)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（三棕之丘——約魯巴宇宙之臍）

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XIII

summary.en: In the beginning all was water, but in the middle of it there was an island (Illa-odo), on which the first chieftains wandered, not knowing what they should do. After a long time Olorun came down from the sky and sat in the middle of the island, the other Gods with him: "Edju, sit thou behind me; thou, Shango, in front of me. Ogun, sit thou on my right hand; Obatalla, thou on my left. Ye other Gods, sit round me in a circle." He called the chieftains: "This city shall in future be called Ife. The hill on which I am seated shall bear three palm trees. Better than in any other place the babalawos will here read the Odus. Sixteen Gods have come with me; these will have children, and they shall live around you. Thus will Ife have a great people. But thou, Oni, thou shalt here hold sway and tell the Alafins what is the will of the Gods." Thus arose the city of Ife, wherein of old abode the sixteen Gods — its hill with the three palms the navel of the Yoruban idea of the universe.
summary.zh: 太初遍地是水，唯水中央有一小洲（伊拉-奧多），首批酋長在洲上茫然遊蕩。良久，奧洛倫自天而降，坐於洲心，眾神隨侍：「埃茹，坐我身後；尚戈，坐我身前；奧貢，坐我右手；奧巴塔拉，坐我左手；其餘眾神，環我而坐。」他召酋長們說：「此城今後名為伊費。我所坐之丘將生三株棕櫚。天下巴巴拉奧讀奧杜，無過於此地。隨我而來者十六神；他們將生兒育女，環居爾等四鄰。伊費因此將有偉大之民。而你，奧尼，你當在此掌權，向歷代阿勞芬轉達諸神之旨。」伊費古城由此而立，十六神舊居於此；城中三棕之丘，便是約魯巴宇宙觀的臍心。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; third Ife creation version, told by a priest from Offa (Frobenius 1910-12). The founding charter of Ife as spiritual capital and of the Oni's mediating role. Cross-ref: yoruba-ife-creation (deep record).

passages.text: In the beginning all was water. But in the middle of it there was an island (Illa-odo). The first chieftains wandered about on it, not knowing what they should do. After a long time Olorun came down from the sky. He sat down in the middle of the island. The other gods came with him. Olorun said: "Edju, sit thou behind me; thou, Shango, in front of me. Ogun, sit thou on my right hand; Obatalla, thou on my left. Ye other Gods, sit round me in a circle."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIII (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Olorun called the chieftains and said to them: "Ye see what there is here. Now, mark ye this well. This city shall in future be called Ife. The hill on which I am seated shall bear three palm trees. Better than in any other place the Baba-lawos will here read the Odus. Sixteen Gods have come with me. These will have children and they shall live around you. Thus will Ife have a great people. But thou, Oni, thou shalt here hold sway and tell the Alafins what is the will of the Gods." Olorun departed. Thus arose the city of Ife wherein of old abode the sixteen Gods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIII (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Farm Stone That Made an Oni: Lajamisan the Usurper
title.zh: 田中一石造就奧尼——篡位者拉賈米散

region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（奧克-阿多加冕丘）

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XIII

summary.en: The ancient shaman of Ife, whose statements Frobenius found reliable, said that the Oni stock itself was in the worst case of all: a forbear of the reigning Oni had been a man from the West who one day found a stone upon his farm, announced that it was the Orisha Lajamisan (an Orisha previously unheard of), and turned it into his own Orisha-father. Then the sly dog deposed the Oni one day and had the Oni-mitre put upon his own head on the Oke-Ado, the coronation hill. Tradition adds that this Lajamisan (Rojamisa) later made a clean sweep of his prelates and patriarchs — driving whole families into exile to Oyo, exterminating others to the tiniest babe — and chose the four highest clan offices from his own family, whose leaders were named Igaru, Agoru, Arrote and Djarra.
summary.zh: 伊費的老巫醫（其言最為可靠）說：奧尼一系本身就是篡奪而來——在位奧尼的某位先祖本是西來之人，一日於田中拾得一石，便宣告此乃「拉賈米散」奧里莎（此前從未有人聽過此名），奉為自家祖神。這滑頭傢伙遂於某日廢黜奧尼，在奧克-阿多加冕丘把奧尼法冠戴上自己頭頂。相傳這位拉賈米散（羅賈米散）事後清洗長老貴族——有的舉族放逐奧約，有的斬草除根——並把四大氏族要職盡數授予本族親信：伊加魯、阿戈魯、阿羅特與賈拉。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the dynastic-origins tradition of the Ife Oni line (Frobenius 1910-12), reporting the memory of an usurpation still alive in the province. Extreme violence reported as the recorded tradition states it, non-graphically.

passages.text: The old man said that many of the others made mutual accusations of having stolen their Orishas and were therefore not descendants of the Gods upon whom they alleged dependence; many were not entitled in any way to make a claim to such descent, for in the earlier warlike times everything got mixed. Both the clans of the Orishas Olokun and Odudua scarcely existed any longer, and they lied who called themselves after these Gods. But the Oni stock itself was in the worst case of all: a forbear of the reigning Oni had been a man from the West, who one day found a stone upon his farm, announced that it was the Orisha Lajamisan (an Orisha previously unheard of), and had turned it into his own Orisha-father. Then the sly dog had deposed the Oni one day and had the Oni-mitre put upon his own head on the Oke-Ado (or coronation hill).
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIII (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: A former Oni is said, at some very remote period, to have made a pretty clean sweep of his prelates and patriarchs: he had driven entire families into exile — they fled mostly to Ojo — and exterminated others to the tiniest babe. More than that, this particular Oni, obviously desirous of throwing off the superiority of his princes, chose the representatives of the four highest offices out of his own family; the names of these four new clan leaders were given as Igaru, Agoru, Arrote and Djarra, and the same informant said that this Oni's name was Rojamisa. Thus the Ilifian Shaman's statement is verified: an usurper named Lajamisan had once cleared the ground, exterminated his most dangerous opponents and appointed adherents of his own clan. He not only killed the previous Oni, but handed over to the son of the deceased the administration of the central quarter of Ife, whose successor is the ninth Agbafe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIII (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Oyo Folk Who Brought Shango Back to Ife
title.zh: 把尚戈請回伊費的奧約人

region.en: Ile-Ife and Modakeke, Nigeria (the twin-city that fought over Ebolokun)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費與莫達凱凱（爭奪埃博洛貢的雙子城）

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XIII

summary.en: The Oyo clan who settled at Modakeke beside Ife — paying their taxes, significantly, not to the Oni who gave them hospitality but to the Alafin — brought Shango, who had been driven forth from Ife, back again, and many Ilifians resumed their ancient Shango-worship. When the Modekans asked leave to hold a great festival for Shango in Ife itself, the Oni refused; families migrated, war broke out, and after years of struggle the Modekans seized Ebolokun, source of Ife's wealth. Then a babalawo in Ife prophesied that the Ilifians would be freed from the evil spirits called Modekans by white people — thought at first to be the Fulbe — and the peace of 1886 restored the city to the Ilifians, who took back from the departing Modekans all the beads they had found in the sacred soil.
summary.zh: 定居伊費西郊莫達凱凱的奧約人——所納賦稅不交收留他們的奧尼，而交奧約的阿勞芬——把曾被驅離伊費的尚戈請了回來，許多伊費人重拾舊日尚戈之祭。莫達凱凱人請求在伊費城內舉行尚戈大典，奧尼不允；民戶出走，兵戎相見。連年爭戰之後，莫達凱凱人奪取伊費財源埃博洛貢。其時伊費有位巴巴拉奧預言：將有「白人」為伊費人驅逐名為莫達凱凱的惡靈——起初眾人以為是富爾貝人。1886年的和約把聖城還給伊費人；莫達凱凱人遷走時，伊費人收回了他們在聖土中掘得的所有珠子。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the Ife-Modakeke conflict tradition recorded 1910-12, before the town's destruction in the 1882 war and its 1886 restoration (also reported by Ellis 1894). Cross-ref: yoruba-ife-creation.

passages.text: A complete revolution took place in the condition of Ilifian affairs when the strange neighbours from Oyo put in an appearance. They paid their rates and taxes — and this is significant — not to the head of Ilife, who gave them hospitality, but to the chief magistrate of Ojo, whom they to the last looked upon as their head. My old Ada-ushe friend said: "The Ojo-folk brought Shango, who had been driven forth from Ilife, back again." They therefore brought their influence to bear on essentially internal religious affairs, and many Ilifians resumed their ancient Shango-worship.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIII (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Modekans one day asked for leave to solemnize a great festival in honour of Shango in Ilife itself. The Oni and his counsellors refused to grant it. In the result a great number of Ilife families migrated to Modeke. This started the quarrel: the prelates declared that the Modekans were to depart from the city precincts; the Ilifians wanted to bring back their escaping citizens by force of arms, and war broke out. The Modekans got the worst of it, but the Oni and his people entrenched themselves within the palace walls, preserved from extermination by a certain reverential awe felt by the victors for the Holy One and the sanctity of his fastness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIII (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: A peace as unsound as possible was concluded; but now the Modekans cast an eye at the source of Ilife's wealth, Ebolokun, and in the second period of dissensions they seized it — it is they who are said to have driven most of the pits which have torn up its soil. The Ilifians never again dug there after that, but when they drove them away took from the Modekans all the beads they had found during their occupation of Ebolokun. At that time a Baba-lawo in Ilife is reported to have prophesied that the Ilifians would be freed from the evil spirits, called Modekans, by white people; it was then thought that these were the Fulbes. They now say, "We were wrong, they are the Europeans (English)." The good offices of the Governor of Lagos ended in the conclusion of peace in 1886; the protocol insisted especially on Ilife's restoration to the Ilifians.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIII (1913); not verbatim.
